newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan president declares famine, scraps taxes.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan president declares famine, scraps taxes.

text.p: President Daniel arap Moi declared a famine disaster in Kenya on Tuesday and scrapped taxes on imported food to help victims, state-run radio and television said.

They said Moi said famine had become a national disaster in Kenya and that duties and Value Added Tax on the purchase of goods such as maize, rice and milk for people hit by the drought would be waived.
"President Moi has declared the current situation a national disaster and scrapped all duties and taxes on food imports," state-run Kenya Broadcasting Corporation radio said.

The step was a climbdown from 1994 when Moi's government clamped taxes on food imports to promote local production and discourage dumping despite pressures from western donors to liberalise the economy.
Earlier on Tuesday, the country's Anglican bishops had called on the government to declare a national famine disaster.

The 21 bishops of the Kenyan Episcopal Conference said a national disaster declaration would make it easier for donors to help and minimise the problem, which they said had taken too long to be acknowledged.
Moi faces a presidential election this year but the date has yet to be announced.
A week ago, Moi ended a ban on the commercial importation of maize, a staple in Kenya which carried a 25 percent tax on imports, for drought victims across this east African country.
The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs said on Tuesday a U.N. assessment mission which toured northwestern Kenya last week recommended an escalated relief programme to address the drought.
The U.N. team recommended the government lift the import tax on maize, make road improvements before the start of the next rainy season and subsidise communities during the crisis period.
The mission noted the failure of successive rains in the northeast had inhibited the growth of vegetation and led to shortages of water for both humans and livestock in the region.
It said livestock prices in the region had fallen steeply and malnutrition and health problems were on the increase.

Earlier this month, the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) asked donors for $12.4 million to buy 25,000 tonnes of maize, beans and vegetable oil to feed distressed people in North Eastern and Eastern provinces for the next six months.
"The situation in 1997 is the most serious since the 1992/93 drought. If the next rains in March and April fail, we have a big problem," Mike Sackett, WFP's director in Kenya, said.
